shots.transcript_text: At dawn on the seventh of June, 1944, a day after the first Allied troops landed in Normandy, one hundred and fifty ocean tugs appeared on the horizon of the English Channel. shots.transcript_text: The blueprint for those floating ports was written in blood on nineteenth of August 1942 on the pebble beaches of Dieppe. Operation Jubilee was mounted by combined operations under Vice Admiral Lord Louis Mountbatten to test whether an amphibious force could seize and hold a defended Channel port by direct assault. Just over six thousand and eighty-six men embarked from England, nearly five thousand of them from the Second Canadian Infantry Division, backed by twenty-nine Churchill tanks.

anchor_evidence.anchor_text: within three hours the raid was a catastrophe

shots.transcript_text: Within three hours, the raid was a catastrophe. Dieppe sat between two steep chalk headlands hollowed out with German gun casemates. On the main beach, loose flint cobbles called churchingle jammed the tracks of the Churchill tanks, while a six-foot sea wall blocked the way into town. Every tank landed on the beach was lost or trapped. By midday, when the surviving craft pulled back, three thousand six hundred and twenty-three men had been killed, wounded, or captured, almost sixty percent of the force.

Across northern France, German engineers had turned Cherbourg, Le Havre, Boulogne, Calais, and Dunkirk into fortresses with demolition charges packed inside the lock gates, cranes, and key walls.

shots.transcript_text: If the Allies could not take a port, they had to land across open beaches in the Bay of the Seine. Yet open beaches posed a severe mechanical problem. Along the Normandy coast, the Channel tide rises and falls by up to twenty-four feet at spring tides, the height of a two-story house. Because the beaches slope so gently, as the tide ebbs, the waterline retreats up to half a mile out to sea twice a day.

shots.transcript_text: A flat-bottomed tank landing ship, or LST, could beach near high water, wait for the tide to drop, and drive its vehicles onto sand. But she was then stranded for ten to twelve hours until the next high tide floated her off. Deep-draft Liberty ships carrying ten thousand tons of shells, steel, and fuel drums had to anchor two miles offshore and swing every crate into barges or six-wheel DUKW amphibious trucks rocking in open swells. One northeasterly gale would halt beach unloading and leave the armies ashore short of ammunition while German panzers counterattacked.

By early 1943, three rival designs competed. The first came from Hugh Iris Hughes, a Welsh civil engineer in London, who proposed towing concrete pier heads, codenamed Hippos, across the Channel and sinking them in thirty feet of water, linked to shore by rigid steel lattice bridges called Crocodiles.

shots.transcript_text: The second design came from a twenty-nine-year-old civil engineer named Alan Beckett, working under Bruce White. Beckett argued that any rigid bridge in the Channel would wrench itself apart when a wave lifted one pontoon while the next dropped into a trough. Instead, Beckett designed a floating steel roadway, codenamed Whale, built in eighty-foot spans resting on pontoons called Beetles.

shots.transcript_text: Crucially, Beckett left the center of each eighty-foot span open so the side girders could twist like a torsion bar. Where standard bridges locked rigid, a whale span could twist by up to forty degrees along its length without bending a single member, riding diagonal swells like a snake's spine. At the seaward end stood a floating steel pier head called a Spud pontoon, two hundred feet by sixty feet on four eighty-nine-foot steel legs. Diesel electric winches let the deck slide up and down its legs as the twenty-four-foot tide rose and fell while ships berthed alongside.

shots.transcript_text: In August 1943, a summer gale roared up the Solway Firth and gave the verdict. Heavy surf scoured the sand from under Hughes' fixed Hippos, tilting the piers and wrenching the Crocodile spans off their bearings. Right beside them, Beckett's flexible Whale roadway rode and twisted with the waves undamaged. The storm also proved Beckett's kite anchor. Shaped like an underwater box kite, its fluke dug deeper into the sand the harder a wave pulled, holding thirty tons of tension where three-ton anchors dragged through.

shots.transcript_text: Inside the walls, Seabees at Omaha and Royal Engineers at Arromanches worked eighteen-hour shifts, winching the eighty-nine foot legs of the spud pier heads down to the seabed and bolting together the half-mile whale roadways to shore. By 16th June, ten days after D-Day, both floating ports were open. At Omaha, an LST nosed into the pier head and rolled 78 loaded trucks down the floating bridge onto French soil in 38 minutes, a job that had taken 12 hours on drying sand. That same day at Arromanches, the 1,500-ton coaster SS Cormount berthed at the pier head and unloaded shells straight onto lorries. 48 hours later, the barometer plunged.

shots.transcript_text: At dawn on 19th of June, 1944, D plus 13, a fierce northeasterly gale of force six to force eight swept down the Channel, gusting to 45 knots. Weather logs showed no June storm like it had hit Normandy in 40 years. Worse, the gale struck at the peak of the spring tides, driving waves 12 to 15 feet high into the Bay of the Seine for four days and nights.

shots.transcript_text: The 96-hour storm exposed a decisive geographical and engineering difference between the American harbor at Omaha and the British harbor 12 miles east at Arromanches. At Arromanches, Mulberry B sat behind a submerged limestone ridge called the Calvados Reef, a mile offshore, which tripped the biggest deep-water rollers before they hit the wall. At Omaha, Mulberry A had no offshore reef. Its caissons stood in deeper water, exposed to 100 miles of open sea.

shots.transcript_text: The collapse at Omaha started half a mile outside the concrete wall along the double line of moored bombardons. Built for eight-foot waves and force six winds, their wire moorings endured seven times their design stress under 15-foot storm waves. One after another, the cables parted. Driven by 40 knot winds and spring tides, 25 runaway bombardons, each a 1,500 ton steel ram 200 feet long, drifted into Mulberry A.

shots.transcript_text: Rather than spend weeks rebuilding Mulberry A's outer wall, Bradley ordered the deepwater piers at Omaha abandoned. US engineers reinforced the inner Gooseberry block ship line at Omaha with supplementary caissons and turned the lagoon into a beaching basin for LSTs and DUKWs. Every intact Spud pier head, Whale span, and Beetle pontoon salvaged from Omaha was towed 12 miles east to Arromanches, turning British Mulberry B into one heavily reinforced port for the beachhead.

shots.transcript_text: Through July and August 1944, as Allied armies broke out of Normandy toward the Seine, Arromanches, christened Port Winston, became one of the busiest harbors on Earth. Using salvaged US spans and 65 newly poured reinforced Phoenix caissons towed from the Thames, Royal Engineers doubled the northern wall, packed the caissons with half a million tons of sand ballast, and expanded the floating Whale roadways until seven miles of bridgework spanned the bay.

shots.transcript_text: Hartley's team built two types of undersea fuel pipe. The first, HAIS cable, used submarine telegraph machinery at Siemens Brothers on the Thames to wrap a three-inch lead pipe in steel tape and wire to hold 1,500 pounds per square inch of pressure. The second, Hamel pipe, wound 70 miles of welded three-inch steel tubing around floating steel drums forty feet high and sixty feet wide, each displacing sixteen hundred tons and named HMS Conundrum. Towed behind tugs, a conundrum spool rotated in the water and laid continuous steel pipe onto the channel floor.

shots.transcript_text: After the war, historians asked a sharp question. Since US crews at Omaha and Utah landed ten thousand to fifteen thousand tons a day directly over the open sand using beached LSTs and DUKWs once the June storm passed, were the Mulberry harbors worth their cost? The official logistics tables compiled by SHAEF and US Army historian Roland Ruppenthal give a clear answer.

shots.transcript_text: Open beaches handled bulk vehicles and rations rapidly in calm summer weather, but they could not lift heavy locomotives, bridging girders, or crated shells without cranes, nor could they work when autumn gales shut the surf zone. At Arromanches, Mulberry B beat its own design target. Built for six thousand tons a day, Port Winston averaged six thousand seven hundred and sixty-five tons a day through July 1944 and peaked at over nine thousand tons in a single day.

shots.transcript_text: More importantly, Mulberry B was the Allied army's insurance against the calendar. German demolitions and resistance on the Scheldt estuary kept the giant port of Antwerp closed until the twenty-eighth of November 1944, nearly six months after D-Day. Designed for ninety days of summer use, the concrete caissons and flexing whale bridges of Arromanches stayed in service for five full months into the November gales.

shots.transcript_text: By the time Mulberry B closed at the end of November 1944, the Normandy beachhead and its artificial port at Arromanches had landed over two point five million men, five hundred thousand vehicles, and four million tons of supplies, including five hundred and twenty thousand tons of direct pier and coaster cargo and two hundred and twenty thousand troops across Arromanches' own floating roadways. Those two hundred and twelve hollow concrete boxes had broken the central premise of Germany's Atlantic Wall. By proving that an industrial nation could build a deepwater port in its own rivers and tow it across the sea, Britain and the United States showed that an invading army no longer had to capture a harbor to liberate Europe. They brought their harbor with them.
